newsitem.title: CHINA: China says North Korean defector spirited out.
newsitem.headline: China says North Korean defector spirited out.

text.p: China on Tuesday breathed a sigh of relief with Hwang Jang-yop, the most senior official to flee North Korea, spirited to the Philippines after sheltering in Seoul's consulate in Beijing for five weeks.
"What I can tell you is that through consultations among all sides, the problem has already basically been solved," Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai told a news briefing without elaborating.
The official Xinhua news agency said Hwang had left China of his own free will after sheltering in Seoul's mission in Beijing since February 12 and had gone to an unspecified third country.

"China, proceeding from safeguarding the peace and stability on the Korean peninsula, according to Hwang's own will and considering the positions taken by the parties concerned, has sent Hwang out of China's territory for a third country," Xinhua said.
Hwang's departure was in accordance with international law and practice, it said.

Even after his departure, security remained tight around the South Korean consular office, where paramilitary police armed with assault rifles and backed by armoured personnel carriers have kept round-the-clock watch throughout Hwang's stay.

Military officers in the Philippines said Hwang and three companions, including at least one South Korean diplomat, flew in to Clark airbase north of Manila on a chartered Air China commercial plane from the southeastern Chinese city of Xiamen.
Hwang was then whisked by helicopter to the mountain resort of Baguio, about 200 km (125 miles) north of Manila.
The defector, who sought refuge at Seoul's consulate in Beijing on February 12, had been spirited to Xiamen from the Chinese capital earlier on Tuesday.

The Philippines offered to host Hwang, North Korea's top ideologue and most senior official to defect from the Stalinist homeland, reportedly because China opposed flying Hwang directly to South Korea.
In Seoul, South Korean officials said Hwang had left China and was safe and secure under their control in a third country.

"With the cooperation of a third country we have him staying in a secure and safe place," South Korean foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung told reporters, Lee said without naming the country. "He's under our control."

North Korea at first accused Seoul of kidnapping the scholarly ideologue and sent scores of diplomats and students to keep vigil around his refuge, but the Stalinist hermit nation later appeared to ease its stance on the crisis.
"There has been no response from North Korea," said Lee, the South Korean ministry spokesman.
"Hwang Jang-yop himself wanted to defect, and the arrangements were made after negotiations with China so I hope no new tensions will develop between South and North Korea," Lee said.

Hwang's defection had muddied ties between China and the two Koreas, bitter rivals since the 1950-1953 Korean War, and forced Beijing to choose between a new capitalist friend in the South and an old communist ally in the North.
On Monday, a senior South Korean official said Hwang would stay in a third country "for a considerable period of time" before going to South Korea.
